target_paper_summary.title: Memory Mosaics At Scale
target_paper_summary.abstract: Memory Mosaics [Zhang et al., 2025], networks of associative memories, have demonstrated appealing compositional and in-context learning capabilities on medium-scale networks (GPT-2 scale) and synthetic small datasets. This work shows that these favorable properties remain when we scale memory mosaics to large language model sizes (llama-8B scale) and real-world datasets. To this end, we scale memory mosaics to 10B size, we train them on one trillion tokens, we introduce a couple architectural modifications ("*memory mosaics v2*"), we assess their capabilities across three evaluation dimensions: training-knowledge storage, new-knowledge storage, and in-context learning. Throughout the evaluation, memory mosaics v2 match transformers on the learning of training knowledge (first dimension) and significantly outperforms transformers on carrying out new tasks at inference time (second and third dimensions). These improvements cannot be easily replicated by simply increasing the training data for transformers. A memory mosaics v2 trained on one trillion tokens still perform better on these tasks than a transformer trained on eight trillion tokens.

target_paper_summary.title: Why Diffusion Models Don'T Memorize: The Role Of Implicit Dynamical Regularization In Training
target_paper_summary.abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of generative tasks. A key challenge is understanding the mechanisms that prevent their memorization of training data and allow generalization. In this work, we investigate the role of the training dynamics in the transition from generalization to memorization. Through extensive experiments and theoretical analysis, we identify two distinct timescales: an early time τgen at which models begin to generate high-quality samples, and a later time τmem beyond which memorization emerges. Crucially, we find that τmem increases linearly with the training set size n, while τgen remains constant. This creates a growing window of training times with n where models generalize effectively, despite showing strong memorization if training continues beyond it. It is only when n becomes larger than a model-dependent threshold that overfitting disappears at infinite training times. These findings reveal a form of implicit dynamical regularization in the training dynamics, which allow to avoid memorization even in highly overparameterized settings. paper_metadata.title: Foundation models for generalist medical artificial intelligence
paper_metadata.abstract: The exceptionally rapid development of highly flexible, reusable artificial intelligence (AI) models is likely to usher in newfound capabilities in medicine. We propose a new paradigm for medical AI, which we refer to as generalist medical AI (GMAI). GMAI models will be capable of carrying out a diverse set of tasks using very little or no task-specific labelled data. Built through self-supervision on large, diverse datasets, GMAI will flexibly interpret different combinations of medical modalities, including data from imaging, electronic health records, laboratory results, genomics, graphs or medical text. Models will in turn produce expressive outputs such as free-text explanations, spoken recommendations or image annotations that demonstrate advanced medical reasoning abilities. Here we identify a set of high-impact potential applications for GMAI and lay out specific technical capabilities and training datasets necessary to enable them. We expect that GMAI-enabled applications will challenge current strategies for regulating and validating AI devices for medicine and will shift practices associated with the collection of large medical datasets. This review discusses generalist medical artificial intelligence, identifying potential applications and setting out specific technical capabilities and training datasets necessary to enable them, as well as highlighting challenges to its implementation.

paper_metadata.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models have been demonstrated to be valuable in different fields. ChatGPT, developed by OpenAI, has been trained using massive amounts of data and simulates human conversation by comprehending context and generating appropriate responses. Eleven categories of failures, including reasoning, factual errors, math, coding, and bias, are presented and discussed. The risks, limitations, and societal implications of ChatGPT are also highlighted. The goal of this study is to assist researchers and developers in enhancing future language models and chatbots. target_paper_summary.title: Optimal Mistake Bounds For Transductive Online Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract:
We resolve a 30-year-old open problem concerning the power of unlabeled data in online learning by tightly quantifying the gap between transductive and standard online learning. In the standard setting, the optimal mistake bound is characterized by the Littlestone dimension d of the concept class H (Littlestone, 1987). We prove that in the transductive setting, the mistake bound is at least Ω
√d
. This constitutes an exponential improvement over previous lower bounds of Ω(log log(d)), Ω
plog(d)
, and Ω(log(d)), due respectively to Ben-David, Kushilevitz, and Mansour (1995, 1997), and Hanneke, Moran, and Shafer (2023). We also show that this lower bound is tight: for every d, there exists a class of Littlestone dimension d with transductive mistake bound O
√d
. Our upper bound also improves upon the best known upper bound of (2/3) · d from Ben-David et al. (1997). These results establish a quadratic gap between transductive and standard online learning, thereby highlighting the benefit of advance access to the unlabeled instance sequence. This contrasts with the PAC setting, where transductive and standard learning exhibit similar sample complexities.

Preserving the Fairness Guarantees of Classifiers in Changing Environments: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: The impact of automated decision-making systems on human lives is growing, emphasizing the need for these systems to be not only accurate but also fair. The field of algorithmic fairness has expanded significantly in the past decade, with most approaches assuming that training and testing data are drawn independently and identically from the same distribution. However, in practice, differences between the training and deployment environments exist, compromising both the performance and fairness of the decision-making algorithms in real-world scenarios. A new area of research has emerged to address how to maintain fairness guarantees in classification tasks when the data generation processes differ between the source (training) and target (testing) domains. The objective of this survey is to offer a comprehensive examination of fair classification under distribution shift by presenting a taxonomy of current approaches. The latter is formulated based on the available information from the target domain, distinguishing between adaptive methods, which adapt to the target environment based on available information, and robust methods, which make minimal assumptions about the target environment. Additionally, this study emphasizes alternative benchmarking methods, investigates the interconnection with related research fields, and identifies potential avenues for future research.

target_paper_summary.title: Elasticmm: Efficient Multimodal Llms Serving With Elastic Multimodal Parallelism
target_paper_summary.abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend LLMs to handle images, videos, and audio by incorporating feature extractors and projection modules. However, these additional components—combined with complex inference pipelines and heterogeneous workloads—introduce significant inference overhead. Therefore, efficiently serving MLLMs remains a major challenge. Current tightly coupled serving architectures struggle to distinguish between mixed request types or adapt parallelism strategies to different inference stages, leading to increased time-to-first-token (TTFT) and poor resource utilization. To address this, we introduce Elastic Multimodal Parallelism (EMP), a new serving paradigm that elastically adapts to resource heterogeneity across request types and inference stages. Building upon EMP, we develop ElasticMM, an MLLM serving system that
(1) separates requests into independent modality groups with dynamic resource allocation via a modality-aware load balancer; (2) decouples inference stages and enables parallelism adjustment and adaptive scaling via elastic partition scheduling; and (3) improves inference efficiency through unified multimodal prefix caching and non-blocking encoding. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets show that ElasticMM outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) serving systems, reducing TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieving 3.2–4.5× higher throughput while meeting service-level objectives (SLOs).
claims: we introduce Elastic Multimodal Parallelism (EMP), a new serving paradigm that elastically adapts to resource heterogeneity across request types and inference stages.

strengths: The core idea that a mismatched training distribution can *improve* test performance, rather than simply degrade it less, is highly novel and counter-intuitive to conventional wisdom in ML.

The paper provides a rigorous theoretical framework to analyze this 'Positive Distribution Shift' across various learning models (power law, memorization, transfer learning), identifying conditions and quantifying the benefits.

The final section arguing that benefiting from mismatch is 'almost always' the case is a bold and significant claim, challenging fundamental assumptions in distribution shift research and offering a new perspective for data curation and active learning.
weaknesses: While the theoretical analyses are strong, the experimental evaluation is quite limited, with only one concrete synthetic task demonstration (skill composition) that could benefit from more detailed analysis and comparison to larger-scale real-world scenarios. More empirical validation would strengthen the claims.

The definition of 'transfer' in Model 6.1 and its connection to Model 3.1 seems a bit hand-wavy. While it states that the transfer term only 'offsets' the final loss and that specific tasks behave like orthogonal ones, a more explicit formal proof or at least a clearer explanation of this equivalence would be beneficial.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative and conceptually bold idea: 'Positive Distribution Shift.' It challenges the prevailing assumption in machine learning that training on a distribution identical to the test distribution is always ideal. The theoretical development is extensive, covering various learning models and providing strong arguments, including the surprising claim that mismatching is 'almost always' better. While the empirical validation is somewhat sparse, the novelty and potential significance of this work are immense. This research opens up entirely new avenues for thinking about data mixture, active learning, and curriculum design, even if the current results are not perfectly polished. I am excited by its forward-thinking nature and believe it will inspire a lot of future work.

strengths: The core idea of integrating LTL specifications with differentiable simulators to achieve differentiable rewards is highly novel and addresses a long-standing challenge of sparse rewards in formal methods for RL.

The proposed soft labeling technique, using differentiable CDFs for AP satisfaction and probabilistic automaton transitions, is a clever and effective way to bridge the gap between discrete logical specifications and gradient-based learning.

The experimental results clearly demonstrate the significant performance gains of the proposed differentiable approach over non-differentiable baselines in complex robotic tasks (CartPole and legged robots), showcasing its practical utility and impact.
weaknesses: While the paper claims correctness is preserved, a more rigorous theoretical analysis of the impact of soft labeling on the overall LTL satisfaction probability maximization, especially in the limit, would strengthen the soundness. The current proof relies on existing work for discrete rewards (Theorem 1) and does not fully detail how differentiability impacts this guarantee.

The reliance on hyperparameter tuning for the CDF function (e.g., sigmoid) is mentioned as a limitation, but the paper doesn't explore its sensitivity or provide guidance on its selection. This could affect the robustness and generalizability of the method to new environments.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative solution to a critical problem in formal methods for reinforcement learning: the notorious sparse reward issue arising from LTL specifications. By cleverly leveraging differentiable simulators and introducing soft labeling for both atomic propositions and automaton transitions, the authors manage to create an end-to-end differentiable pipeline for learning from LTL. The novelty here is outstanding, as it's a bold and forward-thinking approach that marries two powerful but previously hard-to-combine paradigms. The significance is enormous, as it promises to unlock the full potential of LTL in complex, long-horizon robotic tasks where correctness and efficiency are paramount. While some theoretical details on the impact of soft labeling on the asymptotic correctness might be further elaborated, and the sensitivity to the CDF choice could be explored, these are minor imperfections that don't detract from the brilliance of the core idea. The experimental results are convincing and clearly demonstrate the superior performance of the differentiable approach. This work pushes the field forward significantly and has the potential to inspire much future research.

paper_metadata.title: Reward Machines: Exploiting Reward Function Structure in Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods usually treat reward functions as black boxes. As such, these methods must extensively interact with the environment in order to discover rewards and optimal policies. In most RL applications, however, users have to program the reward function and, hence, there is the opportunity to make the reward function visible – to show the reward function’s code to the RL agent so it can exploit the function’s internal structure to learn optimal policies in a more sample efficient manner. In this paper, we show how to accomplish this idea in two steps. First, we propose reward machines, a type of finite state machine that supports the specification of reward functions while exposing reward function structure. We then describe different methodologies to exploit this structure to support learning, including automated reward shaping, task decomposition, and counterfactual reasoning with off-policy learning. Experiments on tabular and continuous domains, across different tasks and RL agents, show the benefits of exploiting reward structure with respect to sample efficiency and the quality of resultant policies. Finally, by virtue of being a form of finite state machine, reward machines have the expressive power of a regular language and as such support loops, sequences and conditionals, as well as the expression of temporally extended properties typical of linear temporal logic and non-Markovian reward specification.

paper_metadata.title: Joint Inference of Reward Machines and Policies for Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling
paper_metadata.abstract: Incorporating high-level knowledge is an effective way to expedite reinforcement learning (RL), especially for complex tasks with sparse rewards. We investigate an RL problem where the high-level knowledge is in the form of reward machines, a type of Mealy machines that encode non-Markovian reward functions. We focus on a setting in which this knowledge is a priori not available to the learning agent. We develop an iterative algorithm that performs joint inference of reward machines and policies for RL (more specifically, q-learning). In each iteration, the algorithm maintains a hypothesis reward machine and a sample of RL episodes. It uses a separate q-function defined for each state of the current hypothesis reward machine to determine the policy and performs RL to update the q-functions. While performing RL, the algorithm updates the sample by adding RL episodes along which the obtained rewards are inconsistent with the rewards based on the current hypothesis reward machine. In the next iteration, the algorithm infers a new hypothesis reward machine from the updated sample. Based on an equivalence relation between states of reward machines, we transfer the q-functions between the hypothesis reward machines in consecutive iterations. We prove that the proposed algorithm converges almost surely to an optimal policy in the limit. The experiments show that learning high-level knowledge in the form of reward machines leads to fast convergence to optimal policies in RL, while the baseline RL methods fail to converge to optimal policies after a substantial number of training steps.

reranking_results.rationale: This paper addresses the problem of sparse rewards in RL, particularly for environments described by LTL-like specifications, which is a core problem the target paper aims to solve. It proposes Reward Machines as a way to exploit reward function structure, offering a different approach to making LTL-based rewards more efficient. It also explicitly mentions supporting temporally extended properties and LTL, making it highly relevant to the problem space.
reranking_results.evidence_summary: Reward Machines (Icarte et al., 2022) propose exploiting reward function structure through finite state machines to improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning, supporting temporally extended properties and linear temporal logic.

reranking_results.rationale: Similar to the target paper, this work focuses on complex tasks with sparse rewards in RL, especially when high-level knowledge is given in the form of reward machines (which are capable of encoding non-Markovian reward functions and relating to LTL). While the target paper focuses on differentiable simulation for LTL, this paper provides a method for joint inference of reward machines and policies to address sparse rewards, representing an alternative approach to improving learning efficiency in similar problem settings.
reranking_results.evidence_summary: Joint Inference of Reward Machines and Policies for Reinforcement Learning (Xu et al., 2020) investigates a method for learning policies and inferring reward machines from observations to address sparse rewards in complex RL tasks.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Traditional reinforcement learning methods often struggle with complex tasks that involve sparse rewards, particularly when safety and reliability are paramount. To address the challenge of sparse rewards in these settings, prior work has explored various mechanisms. For instance, Reward Machines (Icarte et al., 2022) propose exploiting the inherent structure of reward functions through finite state machines to enhance sample efficiency and support temporally extended properties akin to linear temporal logic (LTL). Complementary to this, Xu et al. (2020) investigate joint inference of reward machines and policies to tackle sparse rewards in complex reinforcement learning tasks, offering an iterative algorithm that can learn high-level knowledge from observations. While these approaches enhance learning robustness and efficiency with structured rewards, they do not leverage differentiable simulators directly to convert LTL specifications into gradient-based learning signals to mitigate sparse reward issues.

strengths: The core idea of reformulating De Novo Peptide Sequencing (DNPS) as a continuous mass prediction problem to enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs is highly novel and significantly pushes the boundaries of the field. This tackles a long-standing limitation of current DNPS models.

The use of multi-task learning with a combination of experimental and simulated spectra is a thoughtful and creative approach to encourage generalization to novel modifications, aiming to bridge the domain gap between limited experimental data and a broader theoretical space of PTMs.

The paper provides a strong proof-of-concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search DNPS, highlighting critical challenges and offering clear future directions. This sets a valuable foundation for subsequent research.
weaknesses: The generalization to truly novel modifications on experimental data is still very limited (e.g., recall rates for unseen PTMs remain very low), suggesting that the current approach is not yet robust enough for practical open-search applications. This is acknowledged as a limitation but requires further work.

The evaluation relies heavily on teacher-forced decoding, which, while useful for isolating the model's mass prediction capabilities, doesn't fully demonstrate performance in a realistic end-to-end decoding scenario where error accumulation can be significant. This impacts the practical applicability shown.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative and conceptually bold approach to De Novo Peptide Sequencing by reframing it as a continuous mass prediction task. This departure from discrete token classification is a significant, high-impact idea that could unlock zero-shot learning for novel PTMs, which is a major bottleneck in proteomics. While the current experimental results show limited practical generalization to unseen PTMs on real data, the novelty and potential significance are exceptionally high. The proposed multi-task learning with simulated spectra is a clever strategy, and the paper clearly outlines the challenges and future avenues, which is exactly what one would want from a forward-looking proof-of-concept. Minor quantitative shortcomings in immediate performance are acceptable given the disruptive nature of the core idea and its potential to reorient future research in the field. This work is precisely the kind of ambitious research that pushes a field forward by introducing fundamentally new paradigms.

target_paper_summary.title: Towards Open-Search De Novo Peptide Sequencing Via Mass-Based Zero-Shot Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Proteins are the main drivers of biochemical processes and play a pivotal role in 2 almost all cellular functions. Through post-translational modifications (PTMs), 3 residues within a protein can be chemically modified to fine-tune the protein's 4 function in the cellular context. Despite the importance of PTMs, the plethora 5 of deep learning-based de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) models, which, in 6 contrast to database searching approaches, predict peptide sequence solely from 7 tandem mass spectra without any reference organism database, can only predict 8 peptide sequences with a limited set of PTMs. This is because they rely on fixed 9 vocabularies that map residue tokens to non-generalizable learned embeddings. To 10 overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning. Specifically, we reformulate DNPS as a 13 mass prediction problem instead of a multiclass classification problem, where the 14 model predicts the mass of the next residue instead of its token representation. To 15 facilitate generalization to unseen PTMs, we leverage an adversarial multi-task 16 learning scheme by supplementing the training data of experimental spectra with 17 simulated spectra that mimic spectra containing unseen residues. We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.
claims: we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning.

target_paper_summary.title: Single-Step Consistent Diffusion Samplers
target_paper_summary.abstract:
1 Sampling from unnormalized target distributions is a fundamental yet challenging 2 task in machine learning and statistics. Existing sampling algorithms typically 3 require many iterative steps to produce high-quality samples, leading to high com4 putational costs that limit their practicality in time-sensitive or resource-constrained 5 settings. In this work, we introduce *consistent diffusion samplers*, a new class 6 of samplers designed to generate high-fidelity samples in a single step. We first 7 propose Consistency-Distilled Diffusion Samplers (CDDS), which demonstrates 8 that consistency distillation can be accomplished within sampling contexts in the 9 absence of pre-collected training datasets. To eliminate the need for a pre-trained 10 sampler, we further propose Self-Consistent Diffusion Samplers (SCDS), which 11 performs self-distillation during training. SCDS learns to perform diffusion sam12 pling and to skip intermediate steps via a self-consistency loss. Through extensive 13 experiments on a variety of synthetic and real-world unnormalized distributions, 14 we show that our approaches yield high-fidelity samples using less than 1% of the 15 network evaluations required by traditional diffusion samplers.

target_paper_summary.title: Get Rich Or Die Scaling: Profitably Trading Inference Compute For Robustness
target_paper_summary.abstract:
1 Recent work shows that increasing inference-time compute through generation of 2 long reasoning traces improves not just capability scores, but robustness to various 3 text jailbreaks designed to control models or lower their guardrails. However, 4 multimodal reasoning offers comparatively little defense against vision jailbreaks, 5 which typically succeed by creating noise-like perturbations. When attacking a 6 robust model, vision attacks are also capable of and often must resort to producing 7 human-interpretable perturbations. Rather than operating in a model's blind-spot 8 or out of its training distribution, such interpretable attacks construct familiar 9 concepts connected to the attacker's goal. Inspired by the ability of robust models 10 to force attacks into this space that appears more in-distribution for reasoning tasks, 11 we posit the Robustness from Inference Compute Hypothesis (RICH): defending 12 against attacks with inference compute (like reasoning) profits as those attacks 13 become more in-distribution. To test this, we adversarially attack models of varying 14 robustness with black-box-transfer and white-box attacks. RICH predicts a rich15 get-richer dynamic: models that start with higher initial robustness gain more 16 robustness benefits from increases in inference-time compute. Consistent with 17 RICH, we find that robust models benefit more from increased compute, whereas 18 non-robust models show little to no improvement. Our work suggests that inference19 time compute can be an effective defense against adversarial attacks, provided 20 the base model has some degree of robustness. In particular, layering disparate 21 train-time and test-time defenses aids robustness not additively, but synergistically.

Figure 1: **As model robustness increases, the benefits of inference-time compute on robustness** also increase. A red dot indicates the step at which the model first generates the output targeted by the PGD attack. Robustness increases from LLaVA-v1.5 to FARE-LLaVA-v1.5 to Delta2LLaVA-v1.5.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel framework (AH-UGC) that addresses two significant limitations in graph coarsening: adaptive reduction and heterogeneous graph coarsening. This unified approach, combining LSH and Consistent Hashing, is genuinely innovative and pushes the boundaries of current graph reduction techniques.

The proposed method offers substantial practical benefits, particularly in scalability and efficiency. The ability to generate multiple coarsening ratios without recomputing from scratch and to handle heterogeneous graphs while preserving semantic integrity is a major advancement for large-scale graph machine learning.

The theoretical grounding for load balancing (Theorem 3.2) and projection proximity (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 1) demonstrates a strong understanding of the underlying hashing mechanisms, which solidifies the methodological contributions of the paper.
weaknesses: While the theoretical proofs are provided, their direct implications on the overall performance in complex graph structures could be further elaborated, particularly regarding how well 'similar' in feature space translates to 'similar' in topological and semantic contexts across diverse datasets.

The experimental evaluation, while extensive, could be strengthened by including a more in-depth analysis of the trade-offs between coarsening ratio, information loss, and computational gains for heterogeneous graphs. Explicitly quantifying the 'semantic integrity' preservation beyond classification accuracy might also be beneficial.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a very exciting and forward-looking approach to graph coarsening. The combination of LSH and Consistent Hashing for adaptive, multi-resolution coarsening is a significant leap, as is the explicit handling of heterogeneous graphs. The claim that this is the first unified framework to support both adaptive and heterogeneous coarsening is well-supported and highly impactful. While there could be a slightly deeper dive into the theoretical-to-empirical link and some more nuanced analysis of trade-offs, these are minor imperfections in the face of such a bold and innovative idea. The potential for this method to revolutionize how we handle large and complex graphs is immense. I strongly recommend acceptance.

target_paper_summary.title: Ah-Ugc: Adaptive And Heterogeneous-Universal Graph Coarsening
target_paper_summary.abstract:
1 **Graph Coarsening (GC)** is a prominent graph reduction technique that com2 presses large graphs to enable efficient learning and inference. However, existing 3 GC methods generate only one coarsened graph per run and must recompute from 4 scratch for each new coarsening ratio, resulting in unnecessary overhead. Moreover, 5 most prior approaches are tailored to *homogeneous* graphs and fail to accommodate 6 the semantic constraints of *heterogeneous* graphs, which comprise multiple node 7 and edge types. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel framework 8 that combines Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) with Consistent Hashing to en9 able *adaptive graph coarsening*. Leveraging hashing techniques, our method is 10 inherently fast and scalable. For heterogeneous graphs, we propose a *type-isolated* 11 *coarsening* strategy that ensures semantic consistency by restricting merges to 12 nodes of the same type. Our approach is the first unified framework to support both 13 adaptive and heterogeneous coarsening. Extensive evaluations on 23 real-world 14 datasets—including homophilic, heterophilic, homogeneous, and heterogeneous 15 graphs demonstrate that our method achieves superior scalability while preserving 16 the structural and semantic integrity of the original graph. Our code is available 17 here.

18 1 **Introduction**
19 Graphs are ubiquitous and have emerged as a fundamental data structure in numerous real-world 20 applications [1–3]. Broadly, graphs can be categorized into two types: (a) *Homogeneous graphs* 21 [4–6], which consist of a single type of nodes and edges. For instance, in a homogeneous citation 22 graph, all nodes represent papers, and all edges represent the "cite" relation between them; (b) 23 *Heterogeneous graphs* [7–9], which involve multiple types of nodes and/or edges, enabling the 24 modeling of richer and more realistic interactions. strengths: The core idea of 'simultaneous prior injection and degradation removal (SPIDER)' with prior injection *before* degradation removal is highly novel and counter-intuitive, yet empirically effective. This challenges conventional sequential pipelines and is a bold step forward.

The paper demonstrates impressive performance, particularly on challenging real-world surveillance datasets (SCface), which are representative of severe degradation conditions where current SOTA methods struggle. This highlights the practical significance of the proposed approach.

The use of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for distilling degradation-unaware semantic control tokens and integrating them through a 'decoupled cross-attention' mechanism is a creative and promising way to leverage powerful pre-trained models for BFR.
weaknesses: The description of the 'decoupled cross attention (DCA)' mechanism (Line 129, 189) is very brief and lacks detail; it's central to the integration of the two main modules, so a more thorough explanation or diagram would greatly improve understanding and reproducibility.

While the concept of textual-level degradation removal is intriguing, the exact mechanism for how the 'Degradation Remover' purifies tokens (Eq. 2) and how this aligns with the textual embedding space's 'natural decoupling' could benefit from more detailed explanation and theoretical backing, beyond just empirical observation via t-SNE.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents 'SPIDER', a highly novel and innovative approach to Blind Face Restoration (BFR) that rethinks the conventional sequential workflow. The bold idea of injecting semantic prior *before* degradation removal, and doing so simultaneously at multiple levels, is a significant departure from existing methods. The results on severely degraded real-world data, especially surveillance imagery, are very impressive and underscore the potential impact of this paradigm shift. While some technical details could be elaborated further (e.g., DCA mechanism, exact textual purification), the core concept is strong, sound, and offers a compelling direction for future research in image restoration. I am particularly excited by the potential for this 'simultaneous' learning paradigm to generalize to other restoration tasks. This work pushes the boundaries of current BFR research and should be accepted.

target_paper_summary.title: Spider: Boosting Blind Face Restoration Via Simultaneous Prior Injection And Degradation Removal
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Existing blind face restoration (BFR) methods suffer from drastic performance drop 2 under severe degradations. A common strategy is to first remove degradations and 3 then restore the face by fully harnessing generative prior. However, this sequential 4 pipeline risks discarding subtle but crucial cues from already limited low-quality 5 (LQ) inputs. To address this, we ingeniously introduce a new learning paradigm: 6 simultaneous prior injection and degradation removal (SPIDER). Unlike existing 7 approaches, SPIDER injects semantic prior before degradation removal, thereby 8 preserving identity-relevant features and mitigating the impact of corrupted LQ 9 features. SPIDER consists of two key modules: (1) a prior injection module that 10 distills purified degradation-unaware semantic control tokens from vision-language 11 models, and (2) a degradation removal module equipped with an image-to-text 12 degradation mapper and a degradation remover that refines distorted features into 13 robust representations. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world 14 datasets, including challenging surveillance scenarios, demonstrate SPIDER's clear 15 superiority over state-of-the-art BFR methods. 17 Blind Face Restoration (BFR) is a challenging task that aims to recover high-quality (HQ) face 18 images from low-quality (LQ) ones that suffer from unknown and complex degradations such as low 19 resolution [3, 6], blur [48], noise [13, 28], and JPEG compression [5]. This is an inherently ill-posed 20 problem as the information loss caused by the degradations leads to an overwhelming number of 21 plausible HQ solutions consistent with the same LQ input. To mitigate the ill-posedness, recent 22 studies have explored various prior-based methods to produce high-fidelity outputs. 23 As illustrated in Figure 1, existing prior-based BFR methods fall into three main paradigms: 1) 24 Continuous generative prior (e.g., GFPGAN [36], which learns accurate latent codes via GAN inver25 sion to reconstruct HQ faces with high fidelity; 2) Discrete generative prior (e.g., Codeformer [52], 26 DAEFR [30]), which uses vector quantization to map degraded inputs into semantic tokens and 27 harness a fixed HQ codebook for high-quality restoration; and 3) Diffusion-based conditional genera28 tion (e.g., DiffBIR [18], FaithDiff [2]), which reframes the restoration into conditional generation 29 employing the powerful expressiveness of diffusion prior to achieve significant improvement

strengths: The core idea of 'warm-starting' teacher algorithms with RL agents to address the cold-start problem in human learning is exceptionally novel and tackles a critical barrier in AI in education.

The paper introduces two new environments (Jumper and Emergency Response) and two novel pedagogy-based teacher algorithms (PERM-H and SimMAC), demonstrating strong innovation across multiple facets of the work.

The human subjects studies in two distinct environments convincingly show that RL-initialized curricula can achieve performance comparable to expertly-crafted sequences, providing a practical and impactful solution to a long-standing challenge.
weaknesses: While the concept is bold, the paper acknowledges 'notable gaps between RL agent behavior and human learning patterns.' More detailed analysis or proposals for how to bridge this 'simulated-agent and human gap' would strengthen the methodological underpinnings.

The evaluation, while impressive for a novel approach, could benefit from a deeper dive into the specific aspects of human learning (e.g., knowledge retention, transferability to novel scenarios beyond the test level) that are influenced by RL-bootstrapped curricula, rather than just post-training performance.

While there are recognized gaps between RL agent behavior and human learning, the practical demonstration that RL-initialized curricula can match expert-crafted ones in human studies is compelling. The ambitious nature of this work, pushing the boundaries of how AI can facilitate human learning, aligns perfectly with my prioritization of bold and innovative research. Minor methodological imperfections are outweighed by the potential impact and novelty of the core idea.

paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection via Variational Auto-Encoder for Seasonal KPIs in Web Applications
paper_metadata.abstract: To ensure undisrupted business, large Internet companies need to closely monitor various KPIs (e.g., Page Views, number of online users, and number of orders) of its Web applications, to accurately detect anomalies and trigger timely troubleshooting/mitigation. However, anomaly detection for these seasonal KPIs with various patterns and data quality has been a great challenge, especially without labels. In this paper, we proposed Donut, an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm based on VAE. Thanks to a few of our key techniques, Donut greatly outperforms a state-of-arts supervised ensemble approach and a baseline VAE approach, and its best F-scores range from 0.75 to 0.9 for the studied KPIs from a top global Internet company. We come up with a novel KDE interpretation of reconstruction for Donut, making it the first VAE-based anomaly detection algorithm with solid theoretical explanation.

paper_metadata.title: DeepAnT: A Deep Learning Approach for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Time Series
paper_metadata.abstract: Traditional distance and density-based anomaly detection techniques are unable to detect periodic and seasonality related point anomalies which occur commonly in streaming data, leaving a big gap in time series anomaly detection in the current era of the IoT. To address this problem, we present a novel deep learning-based anomaly detection approach (DeepAnT) for time series data, which is equally applicable to the non-streaming cases. DeepAnT is capable of detecting a wide range of anomalies, i.e., point anomalies, contextual anomalies, and discords in time series data. In contrast to the anomaly detection methods where anomalies are learned, DeepAnT uses unlabeled data to capture and learn the data distribution that is used to forecast the normal behavior of a time series. DeepAnT consists of two modules: time series predictor and anomaly detector. The time series predictor module uses deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict the next time stamp on the defined horizon. This module takes a window of time series (used as a context) and attempts to predict the next time stamp. The predicted value is then passed to the anomaly detector module, which is responsible for tagging the corresponding time stamp as normal or abnormal. DeepAnT can be trained even without removing the anomalies from the given data set. Generally, in deep learning-based approaches, a lot of data are required to train a model. Whereas in DeepAnT, a model can be trained on relatively small data set while achieving good generalization capabilities due to the effective parameter sharing of the CNN. As the anomaly detection in DeepAnT is unsupervised, it does not rely on anomaly labels at the time of model generation. Therefore, this approach can be directly applied to real-life scenarios where it is practically impossible to label a big stream of data coming from heterogeneous sensors comprising of both normal as well as anomalous points. We have performed a detailed evaluation of 15 algorithms on 10 anomaly detection benchmarks, which contain a total of 433 real and synthetic time series. Experiments show that DeepAnT outperforms the state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods in most of the cases, while performing on par with others.
